strengths: Broad and comprehensive empirical evaluation: 11 tasks spanning single-cell analysis (OpenProblems) and scientific deep learning (NASBench-360), with agentic baselines (AIDE, Biomni, ChatGPT-Agent) and expert/NAS baselines, including 3-seed error estimates.

Goes beyond benchmarks: two substantive case studies (improving scDRS with a 40% power gain in simulations, and pgBoost with ~10.5% enrichment gain) that produce interpretable method changes and potentially novel biological findings, demonstrating practical scientific value rather than only leaderboard gains.

Ablation studies isolate the contribution of each proposed component (categories, Bayesian sampling, diagnosis, domain knowledge), and a useful LLM-backbone study shows the framework works with cheap models (GPT-4o-mini at $0.24 per run), an interesting and practical finding.
The system is well-specified (Algorithm 1, prompt templates, code templates, baseline implementations in appendices), and code is publicly released, supporting reproducibility.
Clear positioning against related work distinguishing method development from data analysis agents, and honesty about the concurrent un-comparable work (Aygun et al.).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core components (hierarchical instruction categories, multiplicative reward updates, iterative LLM code refinement with a solution pool, diversity-preserving selection) are incremental combinations of ideas already present in FunSearch/AIDE/DS-Agent/InternAgent-style systems; the 'Bayesian update' is a simple multiplicative decay/reward rule, and the framing overstates its sophistication.

Baseline fairness concerns: Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent were run through web interfaces with only 2-10 iterations within ~1-hour execution limits, versus TusoAI's 8-hour local optimization with hundreds of iterations; AIDE was left at default settings after crashes. This handicaps the agentic baselines and inflates the headline 'average rank 1.2' result. The closest comparable system (Aygun et al.) is not compared at all.

Some evidence contradicts central claims: in Table 3 the 'No diagnosis' ablation achieves the same average rank (2.0) as the full system and slightly better on some tasks, weakening the claim that diagnostic-based optimization is a key contribution; domain knowledge removal also improves ECG (0.68 vs 0.61), suggesting component benefits are task-dependent.

Statistical rigor is thin for the headline claims: only 3 seeds for agentic runs, the blanket claim that 95% CIs are 'all under 0.01' is not substantiated, and the '16% average improvement' figure is not precisely defined. Figures 5 shows non-trivial replicate variance on some tasks (e.g., Decomposition, Visualize).

Novel biology claims (9 new disease-T cell associations, 7 new variant-gene links) are based on FDR-thresholded associations and literature consistency rather than experimental validation, so 'discovering novel biology' is stronger than the evidence supports; risk of optimizing the scoring function to reproduce known gold standards and then re-annotating the same data.

Method hyperparameters (e.g., the 0.1% performance threshold for cluster selection, alpha=0.8, the 1.1 multiplicative update, 10-minute/2-bug-fix budgets) are fixed without sensitivity analysis; the code-diversity metric (TF-IDF cosine similarity) is a crude proxy for algorithmic novelty.

strengths: Broad and mostly thorough empirical evaluation: 11 scientific tasks across single-cell analysis and scientific deep learning, with ablations of each proposed component and a study of 5 different LLM backbones.

System design is clearly described (knowledge tree, hierarchical planning, instruction- vs. diagnostic-based optimization), and the paper is honest about intermediate failures during optimization, including a trajectory analysis of the denoising task.
Two real-domain case studies (scDRS, pgBoost) attempt to demonstrate practical scientific value beyond benchmark scores, with interpretability analysis of the improved methods and cost reporting.
Reproducibility posture is reasonable: code claimed public, prompts and templates are provided in appendices.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core loop (LLM proposes code, evaluator scores, iterate over a pool with bandit-style category weighting) closely resembles existing systems (FunSearch/AlphaEvolve-style evolution, AIDE's tree search, MLE-STAR's targeted refinement, and the concurrent Aygun et al.). The 'Bayesian updates' framing overstates what is in fact a simple multiplicative weight update (pi <- 1.1*pi), and the knowledge tree is a two-level category list — the conceptual delta over prior work is modest.

Unfair baseline comparisons: TusoAI runs 8 hours per task, while Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent are limited to 1-hour runtimes via their web interfaces, and 'best of 10' substitutions are used in deep learning tasks. Compute- and iteration-matched comparisons are missing, making the headline claim of outperforming 'scientific AI agents' weakly supported. AIDE was not given the memory/time configuration parity either.

Results are mixed rather than dominant: TusoAI loses on several tasks (e.g., Batch 0.83 vs. 0.83 tie, Visual 0.44, Decomposition 0.64 vs. ChatGPT-Agent's 0.74, DeepSEA 0.70 vs. Claude-4-Sonnet's 0.73, ECG 0.61 vs. DARTS 0.66), and the 'expert' single-cell baselines (MAGIC, ComBat, logistic regression) are old and weak, inflating average-rank gains.

Task selection criteria involve researcher judgment (excluding tasks with hard-to-reproduce evaluation, excluding metrics with trivial solutions), which raises risk of selection bias toward settings favorable to the method; no held-out or preregistered evaluation is provided.

Claims from the case studies are not fully verified: '9 new associations' and '7 novel variant-gene links' are asserted based on literature consistency, but no experimental or orthogonal validation is presented; the 40% power improvement comes from simulations designed by the authors themselves.

Several presentation/technical issues: the claimed '95% CIs across 3 random seeds all under 0.01' for Table 1 is statistically questionable with n=3; no significance tests anywhere; ablation runs appear to use only a 5-task subset without explanation; Appendix A/B quality is poor (HTML tags leaking into instructions suggests weak pipeline validation).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and important gap: automatically developing and optimizing domain-specific computational methods for science, distinct from both scientific analysis agents (Biomni, Stella) and general MLE agents (AIDE, MLE-STAR), with a clear related-work positioning.

The framework is well-articulated and reproducible in principle: a two-level knowledge tree built from literature, category-level Bayesian utility sampling, diagnostic-based optimization, and a diversity-preserving solution pool, all formalized in Algorithm 1 with sensible engineering details (time caps, bug-fix limits, clustering of candidates).

Comprehensive evaluation: 11 tasks spanning single-cell (OpenProblems) and scientific deep learning (NASBench-360) domains, with strong average-rank improvements over expert methods and SOTA agents (1.2 avg rank on single-cell tasks, 16% average improvement), plus 3-seed CIs and a replicate-stability analysis.

Thorough ablations that isolate the contribution of each component (categories, Bayesian sampling, diagnosis, domain knowledge), showing domain knowledge matters most, and a valuable LLM-backbone analysis demonstrating robustness across 5 LLMs and a striking cost-effectiveness result ($0.24 vs $22.3 for denoising).

Two substantive genetics case studies that go beyond benchmark scores: 40% power improvement to scDRS and 13.8%/7.2% enrichment improvements to pgBoost, with interpretable discovered features (log-log scoring, distance transformations), calibration checks in null simulations, and cost/runtime comparisons to human expert development timelines. The biological discoveries (T-cell subtype associations, variant-gene links) are framed cautiously and supported by literature.

Honest reporting of limitations, e.g., inability to compare against the concurrent Aygun et al. system, cases where GPT-5/Claude-4-Sonnet underperform smaller models, and detailed baseline implementation transparency in Appendix E.
Code is publicly available and the prompt templates and setup details are documented extensively in the appendices, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness concerns: Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent operate under constrained web interfaces (file-size limits, 1-hour runtimes, only 2-10 iterations) while TusoAI runs 8 hours with full control of the environment; for deep learning tasks the baseline is the 'best of 10' LLM generations, which is a weaker comparison. Some single-baseline numbers look implausibly low (AIDE 0.06 on Decomp), suggesting possible setup mismatches.

Several system components are heuristic rather than principled: the 'Bayesian update' is simply a 1.1x multiplier on category weights, and the 'knowledge tree' is two flat lists; the terminology oversells the technical depth, and no analysis shows the specific probability mechanism is superior to alternatives (e.g., UCB-style or simple epsilon-greedy selection).

The evaluation metrics (e.g., modified SVG accuracy, custom normalization of denoising and decomposition scores) were designed/selected by the authors themselves, creating a risk that both the agent and the evaluation protocol were co-tuned; an independent or untouched metric per task would strengthen claims.

Novelty over the closest prior work (Aygun et al., concurrent; AIDE) is incremental — an LLM loop over code with feedback — and rests mainly on the knowledge-tree and diagnostic components, whose individual gains in Table 3 are modest on some tasks (e.g., No diagnosis matches default avg rank of 2.0).

Only 3 random seeds and one optimization dataset per task; given the stochasticity of LLM agents and the visible replicate variance in Figure 5 (e.g., Decomposition spanning ~0 to ~0.4), the robustness of the headline claims would benefit from more replicates and significance testing.

Claims of 'novel biology' (9 new disease-cell-type associations, 7 new variant-gene links) rely on FDR-controlled statistical associations and literature consistency but lack wet-lab or orthogonal experimental validation, and should be tempered accordingly.
Some readability issues: the empty code URL in the abstract, typos in Algorithm 1 ('defualt'), and results for some baselines/tasks left as N/A without full discussion.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper targets a genuine gap — developing new computational methods for scientific domains (integrating unstructured domain knowledge), as opposed to existing scientific analysis agents and general MLE agents.

Technically coherent system design: the knowledge tree, hierarchical planning with Bayesian category-utility updates, and instruction/diagnostic-based fine-grained optimization are clearly specified (Algorithm 1, symbol table, full prompt templates in Appendix U), supporting reproducibility.

Broad and convincing benchmark evaluation: 11 tasks across OpenProblems and NASBENCH-360, comparison against state-of-the-art agents (AIDE, Biomni, ChatGPT-Agent), expert-designed methods, and NAS baselines, with consistent gains in average rank (1.2 for single-cell, 2.8 for deep learning).

Thorough ablation studies isolating each novel component (categories, Bayesian sampling, diagnosis, domain knowledge), plus analyses of code diversity, LLM backbone sensitivity, cost, runtime, and stability across replicates — this goes well beyond typical agent papers.

Strong case studies with real scientific impact: applying TusoAI to scDRS and pgBoost yields interpretable improvements (e.g., log–log scoring, distance features consistent with enhancer–promoter biology) and new biological findings validated at the same standard as the original papers, at very low cost ($0.37–$0.41).
Honest limitations section acknowledging overfitting risks, single-function constraints, reliance on existing evaluators, and heuristic components.
Code is publicly available and prompt templates are fully disclosed, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'Bayesian update' is a simple multiplicative bonus (πc ← 1.1πc) on success; the theoretical framing is loose, and no justification or sensitivity analysis for α=0.8, the 1.1 multiplier, or the 0.1% cluster threshold is provided.

Baseline comparisons have fairness caveats: Biomni/ChatGPT-Agent were not designed for this setting (few iterations, substituted by best-of-10 LLM outputs on deep learning tasks), and AIDE required prompt tuning; the strongest related system (Aygun et al., 2025) could not be directly compared, weakening claims of outperforming the state of the art.

Only 3 random seeds/replicates per task; agentic systems are highly stochastic, so rank differences of 2.8 vs. 4.0 in Table 2 may be fragile, and per-task wins are mixed (e.g., TusoAI loses on ECG and DeepSEA to Claude-4-Sonnet/DARTS).
Metric customization in the single-cell benchmark (replacing default metrics, normalizing scores) introduces potential selection-bias concerns, even if well-motivated.

Novelty of individual agent components (instruction pools, feedback memory, quality-diversity balancing) is incremental relative to FunSearch/AIDE/MLE-STAR; the combination and domain-knowledge integration are the main contributions.
Ablation studies cover only 5 of 11 tasks, and warm-start capability is demonstrated on only a single task (NinaPro), limiting generalization of those claims.
Evaluation on a single optimization dataset per task, with deployment to held-out datasets, leaves open questions about transfer when the optimization dataset is not representative.

strengths: The system is applied and evaluated at unusually broad scale for an agentic optimization paper: 11 tasks spanning two established benchmarks (OpenProblems, NASBench-360), plus two substantial real-world case studies (scDRS, pgBoost) with external validation (calibration checks, gold-standard eQTL/ABC enrichment, literature-supported biological findings).

Comprehensive ablation studies isolating each proposed component (categories, Bayesian sampling, diagnostics, domain knowledge), plus analyses of LLM backbone choice, cost, runtime, code diversity, and stability across replicates. This level of empirical diligence is above the norm for agent papers.

The paper is transparent about limitations (validation-experiment requirement, single-function constraint, reliance on existing evaluators, heuristic components), and the code and prompt templates are released, supporting reproducibility.

Clear positioning against related work: scientific agents (Biomni, ChemCrow, Stella), MLE agents (AIDE, MLE-STAR, R&D-Agent), and classical AutoML, with an explicit statement of what distinguishes this setting (domain knowledge, unstructured search space, warm-start on existing codebases).
The case studies provide quantitative efficiency comparisons (167 variations in 24h at $0.37 vs. months of manual evaluation), which concretely demonstrates the practical value proposition.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty. The core loop (population of code candidates, LLM-based mutation, selection by an evaluator) is essentially AIDE/FunSearch-style evolutionary code search. The two headline 'novel' components are thin: the 'Bayesian update' is a multiplicative 1.1 rescaling of category weights followed by renormalization, which is a naive heuristic multiplier rather than a Bayesian procedure, and the 'knowledge tree' is a two-level list of LLM-generated instructions. Neither is formally motivated or analyzed; the paper itself concedes components are heuristic.

Potential unfairness in baseline comparisons. TusoAI is given 8 hours of unrestricted function-level optimization, while Biomni/ChatGPT-Agent are constrained to 2-10 iterations through web interfaces with file-size and runtime limits; for deep learning tasks, the strongest LLM baselines are reduced to a best-of-10 one-shot sampling protocol. The ablations show most of the gain over a generic loop is modest, and a properly scaffolded AIDE (e.g., with a knowledge base and feedback mechanism) is not tested, so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the scaffolding rather than the name.

Risk of evaluation bias and overfitting to validation. The authors modified benchmark metrics (replacing correlation with accuracy for SVG, excluding several metrics, excluding whole tasks via post-hoc criteria such as 'uncertain about reproducing the evaluation procedure'), and optimization is performed on a single validation dataset. With 8-hour searches over hundreds of candidates, selection on validation combined with author-controlled task/metric filtering raises concerns about generalization, despite the separate test sets. Only 3 seeds per condition.
The most directly comparable concurrent system (Aygun et al., 2025) is not compared against, weakening the central claim of outperforming state-of-the-art scientific optimization agents.

Case study gains, while interesting, are from narrow intervention surfaces chosen by the authors (one scoring function in scDRS; distance features only in pgBoost), so the generality of 'improving state-of-the-art methods' is not established; the improvements may reflect hyperparameter-level enrichment rather than genuine method discovery.

Several claims are overclaimed relative to evidence: 'outperforms state-of-the-art expert methods, MLE agents, and scientific AI agents across diverse tasks' holds only on average rank; TusoAI is not best on many individual tasks (e.g., ECG, NinaPro, DeepSEA in Table 2, where DARTS and Claude-4-Sonnet lead).

Writing/presentation issues: the 'Bayesian' terminology and 'hierarchical planning' framing oversell simple mechanisms; Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse; the abstract claims new biology 'missed by previous methods' based on a handful of discovered links whose validity depends on the same linking-score criterion the system was optimized toward.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem definition: the paper targets a genuine gap between general MLE agents (which assume standard ML setups) and scientific agents (which mostly execute existing pipelines), namely autonomous development and optimization of new computational methods for scientific tasks.

Comprehensive evaluation across 11 diverse tasks (6 single-cell tasks from OpenProblems, 5 scientific deep learning tasks from NASBench-360) with appropriate and recent baselines (AIDE, Biomni, ChatGPT-Agent, expert methods, NAS methods), consistent with prior benchmarking work.

Strong headline results: TusoAI achieves the best average rank on both benchmark suites, and importantly the paper demonstrates that discovered methods are novel rather than re-implementations of existing approaches (with a dedicated appendix justifying novelty per task).

Extensive ablation studies that isolate the contribution of each component (categories, Bayesian sampling, diagnosis, domain knowledge), plus robustness analysis across 5 LLM backbones, stability across replicates, code diversity analysis, runtime, and detailed cost analysis — the finding that cheap low-latency models match reasoning models is interesting and practically valuable.

Two compelling real-world case studies (scDRS, pgBoost) that go beyond benchmark scores: improvements are validated with the same quantitative rigor as the original papers (calibration in null simulations, FDR control, gold-standard eQTL/ABC enrichment), and interpretable improvements (log-log scoring, <50kb TSS indicator) are biologically plausible. The demonstration that methods can be improved on large existing codebases (where competing agents cannot operate) is a meaningful practical contribution.
Strong reproducibility posture: code publicly available, prompt templates fully disclosed, hyperparameters and compute setup documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Several core algorithmic components are heuristic and weakly justified: the 'Bayesian update' is simply multiplying the category probability by 1.1 upon success (a bandit-style heuristic, not Bayesian inference); other design choices (α=0.8 instruction/diagnostic split, Ntop schedule, 0.1% cluster threshold, clustering by code-text similarity) are presented without sensitivity analysis or theoretical grounding, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

Benchmark task selection is a subset (6 of 12 single-cell tasks, 5 of 10 NASBench-360 tasks), with exclusion criteria applied post hoc (runtime, reproducibility concerns); this raises a mild risk of task selection favoring the system, and results are not uniformly dominant (e.g., DARTS beats TusoAI on Spherical, Expert on ECG, and GPT-5 achieves better DeepSEA in the backbone study).

Some baseline comparisons are imperfectly matched: Biomni/ChatGPT-Agent run for fewer iterations/hours than the 8-hour budget, and on deep learning tasks they are substituted with 'best of 10' single-shot LLM generations, making the comparison conditions for scientific agents on deep learning tasks weaker than for single-cell tasks.

Claims of 'uncovering new biology' rest on a limited number of newly discovered associations (e.g., 26 trait-cell type pairs, 7 variant-gene links); while directionally consistent with literature, these are not experimentally validated and the causal simulations used for scDRS optimization partially mirror the evaluation setup.

The framework is limited to optimizing a single function in an otherwise fixed codebase and requires a fast, representative validation experiment; the discussion is candid about this, but it constrains the scope of the central claim that the system performs 'scientific method development' rather than targeted local improvement.

Code diversity is measured with TF-IDF cosine similarity, which the authors admit is a crude proxy; the link between diversity and final performance (correlation 0.519) is suggestive rather than conclusive.
